result: The study analyzed a global dataset of 1303 S. Dublin genomes spanning four decades, including 53 genomes from Australia and 1250 from other regions.
evaluation: Claims C3, C40, C41, C96, C97, and C98 consistently describe the dataset composition and are supported by explicit statements in the methods and results sections. The numbers are internally consistent and the dataset is well-documented.

result: Highly resistant S. Dublin isolates are predominantly confined to North America and linked to IncC plasmids co-encoding AMR and heavy metal resistance, with specific resistance determinants (floR, sul2, blaCMY-2) restricted to North American clade 5.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C54-C59, and C61 are supported by genomic data showing geographical distribution of AMR profiles and plasmid types. The data clearly demonstrate that MDR isolates (632/667, 94.8%) are predominantly from North America, with specific resistance genes restricted to clade 5, and the mer operon frequently associated with IncC plasmids (90.1%).

result: Australian S. Dublin isolates were largely antimicrobial-susceptible.
evaluation: Claim C6 is supported by resistance profiling data showing that Australian isolates had minimal AMR determinants compared to North American isolates, as shown in Figures 3 and supplementary figures.

result: Two phylogenetically distinct lineages of S. Dublin were identified: the globally dominant ST10 lineage (1295 isolates) and the less prevalent ST74 lineage (8 isolates), with ST74 only detected in Australia and distinguished by unique fliC codon profiles.
evaluation: Claims C7, C9, C10, C31, C32, C42-C49 are supported by phylogenetic analysis showing clear separation of ST10 and ST74 lineages, with ST10 comprising 99.4% of isolates and ST74 restricted to Australia. The fliC codon profiles and BAPS clustering provide additional support for lineage distinction.

result: A small number of Australian ST10 isolates harbour a novel hybrid plasmid (AUSMDU00035676) encoding both AMR and mercuric resistance, lacking the spv operon.
evaluation: Claims C8, C63, and C64 are supported by long-read sequencing data and comparative plasmid analysis showing the presence of IncN, IncX1, and IncFII(S) replicons with AMR and HMR determinants but lacking the spv operon, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

result: ST74 exhibited a larger pangenome compared to ST10, with 1143 genes specific to ST74 (including 362 core genes) versus 473 genes specific to ST10, and a minimum of 2402 SNPs separating the lineages.
evaluation: Claims C11, C85-C88 are supported by pangenome analysis data showing distinct gene content between lineages and SNP distance matrix results. The increased genome size and gene content in ST74 are consistently observed across all ST74 isolates.

result: ST74 lacks Salmonella pathogenicity island (SPI)-19 encoding a T6SS, while SPI-6 showed variable coverage across isolates with truncation of the T6SS machinery in ST74.
evaluation: Claims C12, C73, and C74 are supported by genomic analysis and long-read sequencing data showing complete absence of SPI-19 in all ST74 isolates and truncation of SPI-6 T6SS machinery, as demonstrated in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

result: The ST74 lineage displayed enhanced intracellular replication in human macrophages compared with ST10, with ST74 showing up to eightfold increase over 24 hours while ST10 failed to replicate more than twofold.
evaluation: Claims C13, C75-C77 are supported by in vitro infection assays in THP-1 cells showing significantly higher bacterial replication for ST74 at 9 and 24 hpi compared to ST10, as demonstrated in Figure 5A-F with statistical significance.

result: The ST74 lineage induced less pro-inflammatory responses compared with ST10, showing significantly less cytotoxicity and IL-1β release at early time points (3 and 9 hpi) despite higher intracellular replication.
evaluation: Claims C14, C80, C81, C83, and C84 are supported by LDH cytotoxicity assays, IL-1β ELISA, and immunoblot analyses showing significantly reduced host cell death and inflammatory responses for ST74 at early infection stages, as demonstrated in Figure 6A-E with statistical significance.

result: In HT-29 epithelial cells, 6 out of 11 ST10 isolates replicated more efficiently (up to 10-fold) while all 7 ST74 isolates showed minimal replication (up to twofold), with minimal cytotoxicity observed across both lineages.
evaluation: Claims C78, C79, and C82 are supported by in vitro infection assays in HT-29 cells showing contrasting replication patterns compared to macrophages, with ST10 replicating better in epithelial cells, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D.

result: The Vi antigen (viaB operon) was absent in all ST10 and ST74 genomes (1302/1303; 99.9%), with implications for serotyping and vaccine development.
evaluation: Claims C15, C35, C72, and C92 are supported by genomic screening showing the viaB operon was only detected in one historical SLV ST73 isolate from France, indicating the Vi antigen is not conserved in the S. Dublin population.

result: Bayesian phylodynamic analysis estimated the substitution rate for S. Dublin at 1.05×10⁻⁷, with the MRCA of the global population inferred to be 1901 and emergence of major clades between 1950-2000.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by Bayesian phylodynamic analysis using appropriate molecular clock models and coalescent priors, with clear HPD intervals provided. The MCC tree topology is consistent with the ML tree, supporting the temporal estimates.

result: Gold resistance determinants (golS and golT) were ubiquitous in S. Dublin (99.9%), and IncX1 (97.4%) and IncFII(S) (93.1%) plasmid replicons were found at high frequency.
evaluation: Claims C60 and C62 are supported by genomic screening data showing near-universal presence of gold resistance genes and high frequency of specific plasmid replicons, consistent with previous findings.

result: Only 11 genomes (0.84%) had an invasiveness index score <0.5, including three ST10 genomes and all eight ST74 genomes.
evaluation: Claims C66 and C67 are based on application of a bioinformatic prediction tool that was validated on a small reference set (C66). However, the in vitro data (C13, C75-C77) show ST74 has enhanced intracellular replication in macrophages, contradicting the lower predicted invasiveness score. This discrepancy suggests the prediction tool may not accurately capture invasiveness for ST74, or that invasiveness is more complex than genome degradation patterns suggest.

result: Putative virulence factors pagN and pgtE were nearly ubiquitous in S. Dublin, while ST313-gi, Gifsy-2 prophage, and ggt gene were present in ST10 but absent in ST74.
evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by genomic screening showing differential distribution of virulence determinants between lineages, with some factors conserved across all S. Dublin and others specific to ST10.

result: The loss of the spv operon may be associated with a less invasive phenotype.
evaluation: Claim C65 is speculative and based on a single citation. While the spv operon is known to enhance virulence, the manuscript does not provide direct experimental evidence linking its absence in the novel hybrid plasmid to reduced invasiveness. This remains a hypothesis requiring further investigation.

result: The phylogeographic separation and AMR profiles of S. Dublin lineages are consistent with other studies and likely influenced by livestock movement, with historical cattle imports from the USA to Australia in the 1930s supporting the phylodynamic finding of a common ancestor.
evaluation: Claims C89 and C90 are supported by phylodynamic analysis showing temporal estimates consistent with historical livestock movement patterns, though the connection is inferential rather than directly demonstrated.

result: S. Dublin ST74 was previously identified as S. Enteritidis ST74 and sits as an intermediate between S. Dublin and S. Enteritidis.
evaluation: Claim C91 is supported by citation to Achtman et al., 2012, and is consistent with the fliC codon profile data (C45) showing ST74 has the S. Enteritidis-like profile rather than the typical S. Dublin profile.

result: ST74 isolates associated with human disease (n=7) were identified from faecal samples (gastroenteritis cases), whereas 18/40 ST10 isolates were from invasive cases (blood or abscess).
evaluation: Claims C93 and C94 are supported by sample metadata showing differential clinical presentation between lineages, though the small sample size for ST74 (n=7) limits generalizability.

result: The pangenome analysis identified >900 uncharacterised genes unique to ST74.
evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by pangenome analysis data (C85, C86) showing 1143 genes specific to ST74, with 929 uncharacterised genes (1143 total - 214 characterised = 929 uncharacterised).

result: Background claims establish S. Dublin as a bovine-adapted, invasive NTS serovar causing bloodstream infections with increasing AMR prevalence, transmitted through contaminated food, and possessing unique virulence determinants including two T6SS systems.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C16-C30, C33, C34, C36-C39 are background/contextual claims supported by citations to prior literature. These establish the scientific context for the study and are appropriately referenced.
